title: Syntax Constraints Are Not Enough: Semantic Errors Dominate Diffusion LM Tool-Calling Failures

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to test whether constrained decoding closes the diffusion-LM tool-calling gap, specifically addressing the formatting-failure hypothesis. No prior paper explicitly tests this hypothesis or establishes the same empirical relationship between constrained decoding and the tool-calling gap. While several papers (e.g., [1], [2], [5], [8]) discuss constrained decoding for syntax adherence or structured generation, none directly investigate the specific relationship between constrained decoding and the formatting-failure hypothesis in diffusion LMs. Thus, the purpose is **NONE**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves systematically evaluating three decoding conditions (unconstrained generation, best-of-2 with AST filter, and LAVE CFG-constrained decoding with a syntax-only grammar). Papers [1], [2], [4], [5], [6], [8], [10], and [13] all describe constrained decoding techniques, including grammar-constrained decoding (CFG-based) and other methods for enforcing syntactic validity during generation. For example, [1] and [2] explicitly apply CFG-based constrained decoding to diffusion LMs, and [5] discusses constrained decoding for syntax error-free tool use. These papers cover the underlying primitive of constrained decoding, including CFG-based approaches. Therefore, the mechanism is **COVERED**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design measures AST parse rate, parse failures, and overall success rate under different decoding conditions. Papers [7], [15], and [17] describe evaluation setups for function calling or structured generation tasks, including benchmarks like BFCL and syntactic/semantic parsing metrics. For example, [7] introduces IFEval-FC, which evaluates adherence to format instructions in function calling, and [15] uses constrained decoding benchmarks for parsing tasks. These prior works use similar evaluation designs (benchmark families and metric semantics) to validate constrained decoding techniques, even if applied to different datasets or objects. Thus, the evaluation is **COVERED**.

### Domain
The domain is diffusion language model tool/function calling, specifically BFCL-v3. Papers [1], [2], [5], [7], [8], and [17] all address tool calling or structured generation in diffusion LMs or large language models. For example, [7] evaluates function calling benchmarks, and [1] and [2] focus on constrained decoding for diffusion LMs. While BFCL-v3 is a specific benchmark instance, the general application area of tool/function calling in diffusion LMs is well-covered. Therefore, the domain is **COVERED**.

### Purpose
The contribution aims to identify the dominant failure mode of diffusion LM tool calling. None of the prior papers explicitly report or establish the same empirical relationship between parse failures and semantic errors in diffusion LM tool calling. While [11] discusses safety and failure modes in diffusion LLMs, it focuses on jailbreak robustness rather than structured output error analysis or dominant failure modes. Similarly, [9] evaluates multilingual robustness in tool calling but does not identify dominant failure modes. No prior paper directly addresses this purpose.

### Mechanism
The contribution develops an error taxonomy separating parse failures from semantic errors (wrong function, wrong arguments) and tracks their distribution across decoding conditions. [1] introduces a taxonomy of log parsing errors, which is conceptually similar in separating error types, but it focuses on log parsing rather than structured tool calling in diffusion LMs. [3] discusses error analysis in meaning representation parsing, including diagnostic evaluation, but does not explicitly separate parse failures from semantic errors or track their distribution across decoding conditions. [5] focuses on error detection in text-to-SQL semantic parsing, which involves identifying semantic errors, but does not provide a taxonomy or track error distributions across decoding conditions. Thus, no prior paper contains a substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves tracking semantic errors (wrong function + wrong arguments) across decoding conditions and quantifying their prevalence (~60% of outputs unaffected by grammar, wrong-function errors rising from 12.86% to 15.52%, and a 50.74pp gap vs Qwen-8B AR). [8] evaluates non-determinism in diffusion LMs across conditions, but its focus is on dataset-level metrics and non-determinism rather than error distribution. [11] analyzes safety-related failure modes in diffusion LMs but does not use the same evaluation design. [9] conducts systematic evaluation of multilingual tool calling but does not track semantic error distributions across decoding conditions. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of structured output error analysis for diffusion LMs. [8], [10], [11], [12], [19], and [20] all work on diffusion LMs, and [9], [15], [16], [21], and [25] address tool calling in LLMs. While none of these papers specifically focus on structured output error analysis for diffusion LMs, they collectively cover the broader domain of diffusion LMs and tool calling. Therefore, the domain is covered.
